steps.title: Everyday work flows through
steps.talk: Most prompts are ordinary work. AI Guard lets them through with no friction, but it still classifies the topic, so you can see what your people use AI for.
steps.say: Most of what people send to AI is ordinary work, like this marketing request. It goes straight through.
steps.show: ALLOW, plus the topic tag AI Guard added: you learn what AI is used for without blocking anyone.
steps.sowhat: Visibility first: a picture of real AI usage by team and topic, with zero friction for users.
steps.ask: Today, could you tell me which teams use AI the most, and for what?

objections.q: Does this slow every prompt down?
objections.a: Inspection happens inline in milliseconds; the replies you're seeing include the round trip to the model.

steps.filler: We're starting in Monitor, which is where most customers begin: see everything, block nothing.

steps.title: Sensitive data leaving the company
steps.talk: An employee pastes a patient record into a chatbot. AI Guard finds the SSN and date of birth before the prompt reaches the model. We're in monitor mode, so it's logged, not stopped.
steps.say: Now someone pastes a patient record to get a quick summary. Well meant, and exactly how data leaves.
steps.show: The SSN and date-of-birth detectors. In Monitor it's logged, not stopped, so you learn your baseline.
steps.sowhat: You find out how often regulated data goes into AI before it becomes a breach notification.
steps.ask: Which data would be a reportable incident for you if it showed up in a public AI tool?

objections.q: We already have DLP. Why this?
objections.a: Classic DLP sees files and web posts. AI Guard understands prompts and model replies, including attacks on the model itself, which DLP has no concept of.
Start in Monitor, review what fires in Insights for a couple of weeks, then enforce only the detectors you trust.

steps.title: Secrets in a prompt

news.headline: Samsung bans generative AI tools after engineers paste confidential source code into ChatGPT

steps.talk: Developers paste tokens when they debug. AI Guard recognizes credential formats, so a leaked key becomes an alert instead of an incident.
steps.say: Developers paste code to debug it, and code carries keys. This is the Samsung story: engineers pasted source code into ChatGPT, and the company banned AI tools outright.
steps.show: The secrets detector names the credential type. Nothing reached the model's provider unseen.
steps.sowhat: Instead of banning AI, like Samsung did, you let developers use it and catch the keys.
steps.ask: Have you had to restrict AI tools for developers? What would it take to open them back up?

objections.q: Does this work for our own apps and agents, not just ChatGPT?
objections.a: Yes. Your apps call AI Guard through the API or proxy, so the same policy covers home-grown apps, copilots and agents.

steps.title: Prompt injection

news.headline: A dealership chatbot is talked into 'agreeing' to sell a Chevy Tahoe for $1

steps.talk: This is the attack on the AI itself: telling the model to ignore its instructions. It's detected and recorded. Now let's enforce.
steps.say: This one attacks the AI itself: 'ignore your instructions'. A car dealer's chatbot was talked into 'agreeing' to sell a Tahoe for one dollar this way.
steps.show: The prompt-injection detector fired. Still Monitor, so it's recorded. Next we enforce.
steps.sowhat: Customer-facing bots can be steered into saying or doing things on your behalf. That's brand and legal exposure.
steps.ask: Do you have customer-facing chatbots or agents today, or planned this year?

objections.a: Start in Monitor, review what fires in Insights for a couple of weeks, then enforce only the detectors you trust.

steps.title: Turn on enforcement, same prompt
steps.talk: Same prompt, one policy change. AI Guard now blocks it before it reaches the model. Customers usually start in monitor mode, learn their baseline, then enforce the high-risk detectors.
steps.say: Same prompt, one policy change: block attacks. Now it never reaches the model.
steps.show: BLOCK, and the reply the user sees instead of the model's.
steps.sowhat: Enforcement is a policy switch, not a project. Start with attacks, add data protection when you're ready.
steps.ask: Who would own this policy for you: security, the AI platform team, or both?

objections.q: Does this slow every prompt down?
objections.a: Inspection happens inline in milliseconds; the replies you're seeing include the round trip to the model.
Start in Monitor, review what fires in Insights for a couple of weeks, then enforce only the detectors you trust.

steps.filler: While this applies: most customers run Monitor for two to four weeks, look at what fires, then turn on blocking for attacks first, because those are never legitimate.

steps.title: Hidden instructions

news.headline: EchoLeak: one crafted email could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data, with no click

steps.talk: Attackers hide instructions in invisible Unicode characters, in documents and web pages the AI reads. People can't see them. AI Guard can, and it blocks them.
steps.say: The newer attacks don't come from the user. They hide in an email or a web page the AI reads. EchoLeak showed one crafted email could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data, with no click.
steps.show: The prompt looks harmless on screen. AI Guard finds the invisible instructions inside it and blocks.
steps.sowhat: Your AI reads content you don't control. This is the attack that scales, and people can't see it.
steps.ask: Which of your AI tools read email, documents or the web on a user's behalf?

objections.q: Does this work for our own apps and agents, not just ChatGPT?
objections.a: Yes. Your apps call AI Guard through the API or proxy, so the same policy covers home-grown apps, copilots and agents.

steps.title: Risky model output

news.headline: Researchers show Slack AI can be tricked into leaking data from private channels

steps.talk: AI Guard inspects the response too. If a model or an agent returns personal data, it's caught on the way back.
steps.say: AI Guard checks answers too. Researchers showed Slack AI could be tricked into handing back data from private channels. Here the model's reply carries personal data.
steps.show: The response-side detectors. Same policy, other direction.
steps.sowhat: Prompts and responses are both checked, so a model or agent can't become the leak.
steps.ask: Are any of your AI apps connected to internal data, like a knowledge base, CRM or ticketing system?

objections.q: We already have DLP. Why this?
objections.a: Classic DLP sees files and web posts. AI Guard understands prompts and model replies, including attacks on the model itself, which DLP has no concept of.

steps.title: Brand and competitive risk

news.headline: Moffatt v. Air Canada: the airline must honor a refund policy its chatbot made up

steps.talk: Beyond security: responsible-AI detectors flag competitor talk, brand risk and regulated advice. We're back in monitor mode now, and everything we just did is on the dashboard.
steps.say: Beyond security: what your AI says can bind you. A tribunal held Air Canada to a refund policy its chatbot made up. AI Guard flags competitor talk, brand risk and regulated advice.
steps.show: The responsible-AI detectors. We're back in Monitor, and every step is now in Insights. Click Recap.
steps.sowhat: One control for security and responsible AI, with the evidence trail auditors ask for.
steps.ask: Who signs off on what your customer-facing AI is allowed to say?

objections.q: Does this work for our own apps and agents, not just ChatGPT?
objections.a: Yes. Your apps call AI Guard through the API or proxy, so the same policy covers home-grown apps, copilots and agents.

steps.filler: While this applies: everything we just did is already logged with the user, the detectors and the action. That's the audit trail for AI usage policies.
